items.content:
There are two ways AI progress could go very badly and that we must avoid.

First, we could lose control of the future to AI. This is unacceptable; we are unapologetically on Team Humanity, and AI must always serve people. To ensure that, we need ways to ensure that alignment and safety techniques stay ahead of progress in model capabilities.

Second, we could end up in a world with too much concentration of power. If an extraordinarily powerful AI is used by one person or company to impress their worldview onto everyone else, the results could be extremely dystopian.

Avoiding these two threats requires walking a narrow middle path; for example, one country could gain too much power. Another example is one lab ending up with too much power.

items.title: The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especiall
items.content:
The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened. Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot.

We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI. But we do not believe we need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence. Consistent rules to manage frontier risk so that we can maximize the benefits are a good idea (and we are excited by ideas like independent auditors).

Years ago, companies like ours developed things like Responsible Scaling Policies and Preparedness Frameworks. Those were good for that moment, and focused primarily on the deployment of completed models, not what happens during their development process.

Today's shift to focusing on safe development and evaluation will need new tools. For example, at OpenAI we now formulate explicit safety cases in advance of frontier reinforcement learning runs we expect to significantly increase capability, in addition to the safety work we have long done in advance of model releases.

We hope that other companies will learn from our approaches and propose their own; we think shared standards for misalignment, monitoring, and safety will lead to better outcomes. We look forward to collaborating with our colleagues across the industry to formulate the best version of these.

When we talk about “pacing”, we do not mean “stopping”. Progress has been rapid and will continue to be. But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs.

Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness, or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring.

Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves.

AGENT HARNESSES ARE THE NEW GPT WRAPPERS

What exactly is an agent harness? A harness does 4 things:

1. Runs the model
items.content:
AGENT HARNESSES ARE THE NEW GPT WRAPPERS

What exactly is an agent harness? A harness does 4 things:

1. Runs the model in a loop so it keeps working step after step instead of answering once and stopping.

2. Gives it hands to read files, call tools, open portals, and run code.

3. Manages its memory so hour three of a job still knows what happened on hour one.

4. Enforces the rules about what it can touch and when it has to stop and ask a human.

WHY IT'S INTERESTING

- The market is MEGA. I think about it like a wrapper let you sell software ($800B market) but a harness lets you sell the work ($5T+ market)!

- It doesn't depend on any one company's model. The knowledge about the job lives in the harness, so you can run GPT today, Claude next month, an open model like Google Gemma, Qwen, Deepseek etc on your own machine after that, and it keeps working. A wrapper was one model doing everything and a harness is a router.

- It gets better the more you use it. See, every correction a human makes becomes a rule the harness keeps, so what you have after 500 jobs is a completely different product than what you had after 5. Wrappers only got better when OpenAI got better.

- You can charge for finished work! The harness knows when a job is done, so you can price per claim, per filing, per review, per resolved exception, or per closed month. This helps compete with SaaS!

- Most jobs are just the same handful of decisions, repeated, using the same few tools. That's true for most of the 800+ occupations out there, which is why almost all of them could have a harness built for them. Lots of space for startups to be building.

-The frontier labs won't come for these. OpenAI is not going to learn how a freight claim gets denied in Rotterdam or which prior auth your specific payer rejects. Those markets are too small for them and the knowledge only exists inside the job. They'll keep making the models better, which just makes your harness better which is cool.

- OH, AND really important, you can ACTUALLY build one now. OpenAI's Agents API, Claude's managed agents, Vercel's eve, LangChain harness framework etc. They all make it way easier to build agent harnesses. 

Agent harnesses truly are the new GPT wrappers.

This is just the beginning.

The economic model breaks jobs down into bundles of tasks. AI can help someone complete a task faster or better, do the task itself, leave the task untouched, or create new tasks. 

Based on how you expect AI to affect tasks by 2030, our scenario explorer models AI’s potential impact on the US economy.

The scenario explorer focuses on three possible scenarios: modest, substantial, and extreme. The economy grows across all three scenarios. But in more transformative scenarios, AI automates more knowledge work, so the challenge is making sure that the gains are shared across society.

Like all economic models, ours simplifies a more complex reality. But by building better scenarios of our possible economic future, we can take steps to make sure everyone benefits from it.

items.content:
An agent matched human decisions 94% of the time.

The 6% is the interesting part.

A customer of ours has around 150,000 employees and a policy that lets teams request discounts. Marketing wants one for an event. Sales wants one to close a deal.

The volume got so large globally that they had a dedicated team whose entire job was approving or denying those requests.

Before trusting agents with it, they ran a backwards test. Last 30 days, what would the agent have approved or denied?

94% match with what the humans actually did.

Their reaction was not let us automate everything. It was: if we can find the other 6% and route it to a person, we can roll this out.

They now spend about 3% of the time they used to spend on it.

Everyone tells you AI models are getting cheaper.

So what happens if only one of those two curves keeps going?

That decides how much of this ends up controlled by the few, and how much by the many.

items.content:
There is a 24-month window to take a trade that still runs on early 2000s software and give it an AI-native tool.

Restoration work. Water damage, fire damage, mold remediation.

The technician walks the property, takes photos, and records voice notes. 

The report is the handoff between the technician, the homeowner, the office, and the insurance process.

The playbook for one vertical:

1) Pick one niche. I would take water damage restoration and leave fire and mold for later.

2) Talk to owner operators. Read their current report templates. Study the old stack they run today.

3) Build around the checklist that is already in their head.

4) Ship a mobile app that drafts the report before the technician leaves the site.

5) Make it say what is missing while he is still in the house.
- You mentioned the basement, but there are no basement photos.
- You took a photo of ceiling damage, but there are no moisture meter readings.

6) Rewrite the damage explanation in words the homeowner can understand. In a stressful home damage situation, clear communication is part of the product.

7) Sell it with three old jobs. "Send me three old jobs and I'll show you how fast your techs could create reports."

The field report expands into QA, estimates, insurance packets, customer updates, and new technician training.

Start with the report.

items.content:
Every professional service firm already pays a person to read drafts before they go out. 

That job is a local desktop app waiting to be built

Someone writes a client email, a proposal, a memo, a contract summary, an investment note, or an HR note. Then they ask a colleague to check it.

99.9% of firms run this workflow, and it happens constantly.

The playbook for one vertical:

1) Pick one vertical and one document type. I would do email review for independent wealth advisors, not the big banks.

2) Interview 10 advisors. Ask them which emails make them nervous.

3) Collect anonymized examples of the real drafts.

4) Turn their concerns into a review checklist.

5) Build a local desktop tool that checks every outbound draft against that checklist, close to their client data and internal rules.

6) Flag the sentence that costs them the account.

- For a wealth advisor, language that sounds like a guaranteed return.

- For a law firm, a sentence that sounds too definitive.

- For HR, sensitive employee information.

- For an agency, a promise the scope does not support.

- For an accountant, a number that does not match the attached file.

7) Sell the faster first pass. They already ask someone to check the draft.

Same tool works for law, accounting, recruiting, and consulting after that.

Anthropic's Boris Cherny, creator of Claude Code:

"We have no more manually written code anywhere at the company. All o
items.content:
Anthropic's Boris Cherny, creator of Claude Code:

"We have no more manually written code anywhere at the company. All of the SQL is written by models."

He said it on stage at Sequoia in May. Here is the rest of what he said, in 14 minutes:

→ the model has written 100% of his code since last October. a few dozen PRs a day. one day last week: 150

→ most of his work now happens from his phone. 5 to 10 sessions open, a few hundred agents running, a few thousand overnight

→ the thing he uses most is /loop — Claude schedules itself on cron. dozens running at once: one babysits PRs and fixes CI, one keeps CI green, one pulls Twitter feedback every 30 minutes and clusters it

→ every single person on the Claude Code team writes code. the engineering manager, the PM, the designers, the data scientist, the finance guy, the user researcher

→ on the SaaS apocalypse: switching costs and process power stop being moats, because the model ports anything and hill-climbs any process. network effects, scale and cornered resources still hold

→ his one-year prediction: prompt injection defenses, permission modes, human in the loop all matter less, "because the model will just do the right thing"

→ the parallel he reaches for is the printing press. 10% of Europe could read. fifty years later more had been printed than in the previous thousand years, and a book cost 100x less

→ "the best person to write accounting software is not an engineer. it's a really good accountant"

the harness, in his words, gets less important with every model. the thing that stays is knowing what to build.

Boris Cherny at Sequoia AI Ascent, May 2026. Clip is minutes 5 to 19 of the talk.

The YC Summer 2026 batch just closed. Here is the pattern I keep seeing in it.

Three years ago, the batch was dominated
items.content:
The YC Summer 2026 batch just closed. Here is the pattern I keep seeing in it.

Three years ago, the batch was dominated by pure software plays. SaaS tooling, dev infrastructure, marketplaces. The common thread: code is the product.

This batch is different. The majority of companies in it are hardware companies and AI harness companies. Not AI labs. Harness companies. Companies building the scaffolding that sits between foundation models and real-world deployment.

What shifted: the marginal cost of writing software dropped to near zero. A solo founder with Claude Code or Cursor can now ship what a five-person team shipped in 2021. So pure software is no longer a defensible business by default.

The two categories that do have defensible positions:

Hardware, because atoms still have manufacturing moats.

AI harness, because the scaffolding that reliably coordinates models, tools, memory, and human approval flows is hard to build and has real switching costs once it is embedded in a production workflow.

The YC partners are not making a bet on AI. They are making a bet that the infrastructure layer around AI is where the durable value will concentrate.

I think they are right.
